readings.c3s3:
Hurt; injury.

{{smaller block|And [the blow] glauncing downe his shield from ''blame'' him fairly blest.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. ii. 18.}}}}

¶
'''blameable, blameableness, blameably.''' See ''blamable, blamableness, blamably''.

'''blameful''' (blām′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''blame'', ''n.'', + ''-ful''.] '''1.''' Meriting blame; reprehensible; faulty; guilty; criminal: as, “''blameful'' thinges,” ''Chaucer'', Melibeus.

{{smaller block|<poem>Thy mother took into her ''blameful'' bed
Some stern untutor’d churl.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2.}}}}

'''2.''' Faultfinding; blaming: as, a ''blameful'' look or word. ''Ruskin.''

'''blamefully''' (blām′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a blameful manner.

'''blamefulness''' (blām′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' [< ''blameful'' + ''-ness''.] The state of being blameful.

'''blameless''' (blām′les), ''a.'' [ME. ''blameles''; < ''blame'' + ''-less''.] Not meriting blame or censure; without fault; undeserving of reproof; innocent; guiltless: as, “the ''blameless'' Indians,” ''Thomson'', Memory of Lord Talbot.

{{smaller block|We will be ''blameless'' of this thine oath. {{right|Josh. ii. 17.}}
<poem>Wearing the white flower of a ''blameless'' life.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Ded. of Idylls.}}}}

{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' Faultless, irreproachable, unimpeachable, unsullied, spotless, stainless, unblemished.}}

'''blamelessly''' (blām′les-li), ''adv.'' In a blameless manner; without fault or crime; innocently.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|blade|575|blamelessly}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|<poem>If ere your ''blades''
Had point or prowess, prove them now.</poem>
{{right|''Moore'', Lalla Rookh.}}}}
{{smaller block|The famous Damascus ''blades'', so renowned in the time of the Crusaders, are made here no longer.
{{right|''B. Taylor'', Lands of the Saracen, p. 130.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') The broad, flattened part of certain instruments and utensils, as of an oar, a paddle, a spade, etc.}}
{{smaller block|The ''blade'' of her light oar threw off its shower of spray.
{{right|''Whittier'', Bridal of Pennacook.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') A broad flattened part of a bone: as, a jaw-''blade''; specifically, the scapula or shoulder-blade.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Atrides’ lance did gore
Pylæmen’s shoulder in the ''blade''.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, v.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') The front flat part of the tongue.   ''H. Sweet'', Handbook of Phonetics. (''e'') A commercial name for the four large plates on the sides, and the five large plates in the middle, of the upper shell of the sea-turtle, which yield the best tortoise-shell. (''f'') That limb of a level which is movable on a pivot at the joint, in order that it may be adjusted to include any angle between it and the stock. (''g'') The float or vane of a propeller or paddle-wheel. (''h'') The web or plate of a saw. (''i'') The edge of a sectorial tooth. (''j'') In ''entom.'', one of the flat, two-edged plates forming the sword-like ovipositor of certain ''Orthoptera'' and ''Homoptera''; in a wider sense, the ovipositor itself.}}
'''4.''' A dashing or rollicking fellow; a swaggerer; a rakish fellow; strictly, perhaps, one who is sharp and wide awake: as, “jolly ''blades'',” ''Evelyn'', Memoirs, i.
{{smaller block|The soldiers of the city, valiant ''blades''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|A brisk young fellow, with his hat cocked like a fool behind, as the present fashion among the ''blades'' is.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, III. 142.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He saw a turnkey in a trice
Fetter a troublesome ''blade''.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', The Devil’s Thoughts.}}}} '''5.''' One of the principal rafters of a roof.   ''Gwilt.''

To take off the blades of (herbs). [Now only prov. Eng.]—'''2.''' To furnish with a blade; fit a blade to.—{{smaller|'''To blade it†''', to fight with blades or swords.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To come into blade; produce blades.
{{smaller block|<poem>As sweet a plant, as fair a flower is faded,
As ever in the Muse’s garden ''bladed.''</poem>

'''blamable, blameable''' (blā′mạ-bl), ''a.''   [< ''blame'' + ''-able.'']   Deserving of blame or censure; faulty; culpable; reprehensible; censurable.
{{smaller block|Such feelings, though ''blamable'', were natural and not wholly inexcusable.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}}

'''blamableness, blameableness''' (blā′mạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being blamable; culpability; faultiness.
{{smaller block|If we are to measure degrees of ''blameableness'', one wrong must be set off against the other.
{{right|''Edinburgh Rev.'', CLXIV. 450.}}}}

'''blamably, blameably''' (blā′mạ-bli), ''adv.'' In a blamable manner; culpably.
{{smaller block|I . . . took occasion to observe, that the world in general began to be ''blameably'' indifferent as to doctrinal matters.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xiv.}}}}

'''blame''' (blām), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''blamed'', ppr. ''blaming''.   [< ME. ''blamen'' = MD. ''blamen'' (also ''blameren'', D. ''blameren''), < OF. ''blasmer'', ''blamer'', F. ''blâmer'' = Pr. ''blasmar'' = OSp. ''blasmar'' = It. ''biasimare'', < LL. ''blasphemare'', speak ill of, blame, also blaspheme, < Gr. βλασφημεῖν, speak ill, whence the full E. form ''blaspheme'', q. v.]   '''1.''' To express disapprobation of; find fault with; censure: opposed to ''praise'' or ''commend''.
{{smaller block|No lesse is to be ''blam’d'' their odd pronouncing of Latine, so that out of England none were able to understand or endure it.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, May 13, 1661.}}}}
{{smaller block|We ''blamed'' him, and with perfect justice and propriety, for saying what he did not mean.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Sadler’s Ref. Refuted.}}}} Formerly it might be followed by ''of''.
{{smaller block|Tomoreus he ''blam’d of'' inconsiderate rashness.
{{right|''Knolles'', Hist. Turks.}}}}
'''2.''' To charge; impute as a fault; lay the responsibility of: as, he ''blames'' the failure on you. [Colloq.]—'''3†.''' To bring reproach upon; blemish; injure.
{{smaller block|<poem>This ill state in which she stood;
To which she for his sake had weetingly
Now brought herselfe, and ''blam’d'' her noble blood.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. iii. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|[In such phrases as ''he is to blame'', ''to blame'', by an old and common construction, has the passive meaning ‘to be blamed, blamable.’ Compare ''a house to let, hire, build; grain ready to cut'', etc.
<poem>You were ''to blame'', I must be plain with you.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I was ''to blame'' to be so rash; I am sorry.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|In writers of the Elizabethan period it was often written ''too blame'', ''blame'' apparently being mistaken for an adjective.]}}
='''Syn. 1.''' To reprove, reproach, chide, upbraid, reprehend. See ''decry''.

'''blame''' (blām), ''n.''   [< ME. ''blame'' = MD. ''blame'', D. ''blaam'', < OF. ''blasme'', F. ''blâme'' (= Pr. ''blasme'' = OSp. Pg. ''blasmo'' = It. ''biasimo''), < ''blasmer'', v., blame: see ''blame'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' An expression of disapproval of something deemed to be wrong; imputation of a fault; censure; reprehension.
{{smaller block|Let me bear the ''blame'' for ever. {{right|Gen. xliii. 9.}}}}
'''2.''' That which is deserving of censure or disapprobation; fault; crime; sin.
{{smaller block|That we should be holy and without ''blame'' before him.
{{right|Eph. i. 4.}}}}
'''3.''' Culpability; responsibility for something that is wrong: as, the ''blame'' is yours.—'''4†.''' Hurt; injury.

{{smaller block|And [the blow] glauncing downe his shield from ''blame'' him fairly blest.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. ii. 18.}}}}

'''blameable, blameableness, blameably.''' See ''blamable, blamableness, blamably''.

'''blameful''' (blām′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''blame'', ''n.'', + ''-ful''.]   '''1.''' Meriting blame; reprehensible; faulty; guilty; criminal: as, “''blameful'' thinges,” ''Chaucer'', Melibeus.

<poem>Thy mother took into her ''blameful'' bed
Some stern untutor’d churl.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2.}}}}

'''2.''' Faultfinding; blaming: as, a ''blameful'' look or word.   ''Ruskin.''

'''blamefully''' (blām′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a blameful manner.

'''blamefulness''' (blām′fu̇l-nes), ''n.''   [< ''blameful'' + ''-ness''.]   The state of being blameful.

'''blameless''' (blām′les), ''a.''   [ME. ''blameles''; < ''blame'' + ''-less''.]   Not meriting blame or censure; without fault; undeserving of reproof; innocent; guiltless: as, “the ''blameless'' Indians,” ''Thomson'', Memory of Lord Talbot.

{{smaller block|We will be ''blameless'' of this thine oath. {{right|Josh. ii. 17.}}}}
<poem>Wearing the white flower of a ''blameless'' life.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Ded. of Idylls.}}}}

{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' Faultless, irreproachable, unimpeachable, unsullied, spotless, stainless, unblemished.}}

'''blamelessly''' (blām′les-li), ''adv.'' In a blameless manner; without fault or crime; innocently.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
